# Kaṇḍarījātaka (Ja 341)

**ID:** Ja 341
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Kaṇḍarījātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kaṇḍarījātaka* (Ja 341) is a birth story located in the *Kokilavagga* of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1883]. In the canonical and commentary arrangement at this location, the story itself is not presented in full; rather, the text explicitly notes that the detailed narrative (*vitthārakathā*) is set forth in the *Kuṇālajātaka* (Ja 536) [Fausböll 1883].

As recorded in the Kuṇālajātaka commentary and discussed in secondary scholarship, the narrative concerns King Kaṇḍarī of Bārāṇasī, his wife Queen Kinnarā, and the king's wise chaplain (*purohita*) Pañcālacanda [Fausböll 1891; Riccardi]. Queen Kinnarā betrays and leaves her husband for a cripple (*pīṭhasappi*), forming one of several misogynous narratives collected in the Kuṇāla birth story [Fausböll 1891; Riccardi]. Discussing the textual history of the story, Heinrich Lüders and Willem Bollée noted that the compound *Kandarikannarānam* was misdivided as *Kandari-kinnarānam*, giving the title *Kandari-jātaka* to what had once been an independent jātaka [Riccardi]. Bollée also observed that the tale circulated widely and reached Nepal, where it was recited by Newar Vajrācāryas [Riccardi].

**Sources**

- [Fausböll 1883] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 3 (London: Trübner & Co., 1883) — Placement in Kokilavagga and commentarial reference deferring the narrative to Kuṇālajātaka.
- [Fausböll 1891] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 5 (London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co., 1891) — Full narrative text and verse regarding King Kaṇḍarī, Queen Kinnarā, and the cripple.
- [Riccardi] Theodore Riccardi, Jr., Buddhism in Ancient and Medieval Nepal — Discussion of the tale's misogynous themes, Lüders and Bollée's analysis of the title's transmission, and evidence of the story in Nepal.
